docs.title: Card Provisioning
docs.text: Add Adyen-issued payment cards to Google Wallet directly from your Android application.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Card Provisioning lets cardholders add an existing Adyen-issued payment card to Google Wallet. Under the hood, the flow provisions network tokens for wallet payments. It does not issue a new payment card.

The SDKs in this family check eligibility, exchange opaque payment data with Google's Push Provisioning API, and report the final state to your app without exposing plaintext card credentials.

Two SDK variants are offered. Pick the one that fits your backend integration.

docs.title: SDKs in this family
docs.text: Card Provisioning Sessions Card Provisioning (Offline) Recommended for new integrations A session-scoped variant where the SDK manages the back-and-forth with Adyen on your behalf, reducing the surface area your backend has to expose. The original integration: your backend exchanges sdkInput / sdkOutput opaque blobs with Adyen, and the SDK drives the wallet flow on the device. Full control over network calls and credential handling. “Offline” means the SDK does not call Adyen directly, not that provisioning works without an internet connection. Open the SDK guide → Open the SDK guide →

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text: Concern Card Provisioning Sessions Card Provisioning (Offline) Who does the networking The SDK communicates directly with Adyen; your backend provides session tokens Your backend calls Adyen; your app passes sdkInput and sdkOutput between your backend and the SDK Backend → Adyen calls Session-token requests on demand via SessionTokenProvider, not just once per session; return a fresh token on every invocation One GET and one POST networkTokenActivationData call per card Application certificate Required (Adyen-issued .cer, embedded in res/raw) Not required Multi-card per instance Yes — one session covers a Set<String> of payment instruments No — one CardProvisioning instance per card Tamper detection signals Built in — TamperError result variant Not surfaced Migration From Card Provisioning (Offline) From pre-0.4.0

docs.title: Example App
docs.text:
This app demonstrates both Adyen Card Provisioning integrations for Google Wallet:

  • Card Provisioning Sessions, recommended for new integrations and selected by default.
  • Card Provisioning (Offline), for backends that manage the activation-data exchange directly.

The segmented buttons switch between the two integrations.

Non-functional reference. This app shows how to add card provisioning to your own app. It uses in-memory fakes and a placeholder certificate, does not connect to a backend, and cannot provision cards. Your integration uses your own backend and the application certificate Adyen issues for your app.

docs.title: Sessions integration
docs.text:
provisioningsessions/repository/ProvisioningSessionsRepository.kt demonstrates:

  1. Creating a session with an application Context and ProvisioningSessionConfiguration containing DER-encoded certificate bytes, payment-instrument IDs and SessionEnvironment.Test.
  2. Wrapping each fresh backend token in SessionToken inside the SessionTokenProvider callback. Tokens must not be cached. The SDK retries provider exceptions up to twice; a returned token that fails local validation is not retried.
  3. Calling provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId) and handling CanProvision, Provisioned and CannotProvision.
  4. Calling provisionCard(paymentInstrumentId, cardDisplayName, cardAddress) without a per-step OPC callback. The display name is a card label, not the cardholder's name.
  5. Handling TamperError from either operation by invalidating the user's backend session, blocking further operations, and showing neutral UI without the tamper code.

Your app needs to support two backend operations for this flow:

  • Fetch a fresh session token on demand, scoped to the requested payment instruments and the Network Token: Create role. Keep your Adyen API key on the backend, never in the app.
  • Invalidate or revoke the user's session on your backend when handling a TamperError. A production backend should make revocation reliable even if the device loses connectivity.

The example groups these operations in a SessionsBackend interface with suspend functions, as one possible coroutine-based implementation. This is application code, not an Adyen SDK type or a required class or set of method names; structure these backend calls to fit your app. See Getting Started for token-provider behavior and failure handling.

For the rest of the integration setup:

  • Embed the certificate Adyen issues for your app's applicationId. The bundled res/raw/fake_app_cert.cer is a placeholder; MainActivity converts it to the DER bytes the SDK configuration accepts.
  • Match SessionEnvironment to your backend's session host. This example explicitly uses Test; use Live for production and Beta only when directed by Adyen.

See Getting Started for the session request body, host URLs and complete result-type guidance. Backend failures can carry an optional traceId for support. This example displays generic messages rather than exposing raw backend errors; production diagnostics should retain only safe result categories and correlation IDs, never tokens or payloads.

docs.title: Direct SDK integration
docs.text: provisioningsdk/repository/ProvisioningSdkRepository.kt demonstrates fetching activation data from your backend, creating a CardProvisioning client, calling canProvision() and then provision(...) with an OpcProvider. The provider sends the opaque sdkOutput to your backend and returns the matching opaque card data. Return within 20 seconds and do not retry a single-use sdkOutput. FakeSdkBackend illustrates the payload shape but cannot provision a real card.

docs.title: Lifecycle and UI
docs.text: MainViewModel holds the repositories across rotation. ResumedActivityProvider keeps only a weak reference to the currently resumed Activity, updated from MainActivity.onResume() and cleared in onPause(). Both SDKs resolve the host on demand rather than retaining the Activity that created the ViewModel. Provisioning disables repeated taps and mode switching until the operation completes. Cancellation propagates rather than being shown as an error.

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
1. Open the project in Android Studio. Use JDK 17 or a newer JDK supported by the project's Gradle version. The Java and Kotlin compilation targets remain Java 17.
  2. Build with ./gradlew :example:assembleDebug.
  3. Run on a physical Android device with Google Play services. The app requires Android 12 (API 31) or later. This minimum applies to the example app; the SDKs support Android 8.0 (API 26) or later. Emulators are not supported for SDK operations.

Your own app must also be allowlisted by Google.

From version 0.6.0 onward, provisioning-sdk includes Google's Tap and Pay library. You do not need to download or host that library separately. The public example resolves provisioning-sdk and provisioning-sessions from Maven Central at the coordinated SDK version.

Run example checks with ./gradlew :example:testDebugUnitTest :example:lintDebug. The example is illustrative, not a prescribed production architecture. Never log or hardcode real tokens, activation data or API credentials. Review the Security Guide before adapting it to your banking application.

docs.title: Google Push Provisioning API Access
docs.text:
Both SDKs in the Card Provisioning family rely on Google's Push Provisioning API, provided by Google's Tap and Pay SDK (com.google.android.gms:play-services-tapandpay version 18.10.0), which is not published to any public Maven repository. From version 0.6.0 onward, provisioning-sdk includes Google's Tap and Pay library, so you do not need to download or host that library separately. If your build previously declared a direct play-services-tapandpay dependency for the SDK, you can remove it — provided no other part of your app uses the library.

Before integrating either SDK, your app must be allowlisted by Google. For release 0.6.0 and later, the allowlisting step below is the only setup required: it is a one-time step that applies to whichever SDK you integrate. Only apps integrating a release older than 0.6.0, or calling Google's Push Provisioning API directly outside the Adyen SDK, will need to additionally obtain and host the artifact themselves.

docs.title: Get your app allowlisted by Google
docs.text:
Upgrading from legacy Tap and Pay

Existing allowlisting for Google's legacy Tap and Pay push-provisioning API does not carry over to Unified Push Provisioning (UPP). If your app was previously approved for the legacy API, request allowlisting again for UPP before using SDK version 0.6.0 or later.

Your Adyen Project Operations Manager or Implementation Manager can initiate this, or you can request allowlisting directly from Google. You will need to provide:

  • Your app's package name(s)
  • The SHA-256 signing certificate fingerprint for every build variant that will use the SDK

Note

Allowlisting is per package name + signing certificate. Add every developer machine certificate, every CI signing certificate, and every release certificate that will produce builds calling into the SDK.

docs.title: Finding your app's package name
docs.text:
The package name is the applicationId declared in your app module's build.gradle.kts (or build.gradle):

android {
    defaultConfig {
        applicationId = "com.example.yourapp"
        // …
    }
}

If you use product flavors or per-build-type applicationIdSuffixes, every resulting applicationId must be allowlisted separately.

docs.title: Finding the SHA-256 signing certificate fingerprint
Developer and CI builds (local keystores)
docs.text:
Run the signingReport Gradle task against your app module — either from Android Studio's Gradle pane (:app → Tasks → android → signingReport) or from a terminal:

./gradlew :app:signingReport

The task prints MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-256 fingerprints for each variant + keystore it can resolve. Copy the SHA-256 value for every variant you need allowlisted (typically debug for each developer machine, plus any release variant signed with a CI or release keystore).

docs.title: Google Play app signing (Play Console)
docs.text:
If you publish through Google Play and use Play App Signing, Google re-signs your release builds with an app signing key they manage. The SHA-256 of that key is not in your local keystore — you must retrieve it from the Play Console:

  1. Open the Play Console and select your app.
  2. Navigate to Protected with Play → Play Store protection → Manage Play app signing.
  3. Scroll to App signing key and copy the SHA-256 certificate fingerprint from the app signing certificate. This is the fingerprint to allowlist for end-user devices that install your app from Google Play.

Google periodically updates the Play Console navigation, so menu names and the location of this page may change. Look for the App signing page and the app signing key certificate, rather than the upload key certificate.

If multiple app signing certificates are listed, include the SHA-256 fingerprints for all certificates used to sign builds delivered to your supported devices.

The same screen also lists the upload key certificate fingerprint (matching the keystore you sign uploads with). You do not need that for end-user allowlisting, but it can be useful when reconciling CI keystores.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Common issues encountered when integrating the Card Provisioning SDKs (the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK and the offline provisioning SDK), and how to resolve them.

Unless otherwise noted, every entry on this page applies to both SDKs — the underlying Google Tap and Pay integration, allowlisting requirements, and Google Wallet behaviour are shared.

docs.title: Google Tap and Pay dependency not found
docs.text:
From 0.6.0, the published offline provisioning SDK artifact bundles com.google.android.gms:play-services-tapandpay. This also applies when using the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK, which depends on provisioning-sdk. Integrations no longer need to obtain or host this library separately unless their own code uses it directly.

A resolution failure therefore has one of two causes:

  • You are using 0.4.1 or earlier. These versions require the Tap and Pay artifact to be obtained through Google's allowlisting process and hosted in your local Maven cache or an internal repository (never a public one). Upgrade to 0.6.0 or later to use the bundled library.
  • Your own build still declares a direct play-services-tapandpay dependency. Gradle resolves every dependency your build declares, and the copy bundled in the Adyen SDK does not satisfy it. If only the Adyen SDK used the library, remove the declaration after upgrading to 0.6.0 or later. If your own code uses it, you still need authorized access to the artifact.

See Google Push Provisioning API Access for the allowlisting setup. App allowlisting is still required regardless of SDK version. Existing allowlisting for Google's legacy Tap and Pay push-provisioning API does not carry over to Unified Push Provisioning (UPP). If your app was previously approved for the legacy API, request allowlisting again for UPP before using SDK version 0.6.0 or later.

docs.title: API calls fail with error code 15009
docs.text:
A 15009 status code returned from a Google Tap and Pay API call indicates the calling app is not allowlisted by Google for the Push Provisioning API. Verify that the package name and the SHA-256 signing certificate fingerprint of the build you are running have both been registered through the Push Provisioning API allowlist process.

The allowlist is per package name + signing certificate, so every distinct certificate that will produce builds calling into the SDK has to be enrolled separately. In practice that means:

How the build is produced or installed Certificate to allowlist Where to find the SHA-256 Local build on a developer machine That machine's debug keystore — one per developer ./gradlew :app:signingReport CI build The CI signing keystore ./gradlew :app:signingReport, or your CI keystore configuration Release build signed locally Your release keystore ./gradlew :app:signingReport Installed from Google Play — internal, closed, open testing or production The Play App Signing app signing key (Google re-signs the upload, so this is not your upload key) Play Console → Google Play app signing Shared via an internal app sharing link The Play-generated internal test certificate Play Console → Test and release → Internal testing → Internal app sharing → Uploaders and testers, under Internal test certificate

Play testing and production tracks normally use the app signing key. If you have upgraded that key, Play may sign builds with different keys for different Android versions. Allowlist every app signing certificate used for supported devices.

Note

Internal app sharing is the case most often missed. Play Console generates a dedicated internal test certificate for your app and re-signs every internal app sharing upload with it, regardless of which key you signed with — so its fingerprint differs from both your upload key and your app signing key. Until it is allowlisted, a build shared over an internal app sharing link fails with 15009 even though the identical code provisions correctly when installed from a test track.

See Google Push Provisioning API Access for the full prerequisites.

docs.title: Provisioning fails because the wallet is not supported
docs.text: The Card Provisioning Sessions SDK returns ProvisioningState.CannotProvision.WalletNotSupported when the card cannot be added to the wallet, or ProvisionResult.Failure.TapAndPayNotAvailable when the app cannot call the Tap and Pay API. The offline provisioning SDK uses GooglePayNotSupported for the equivalent creation failure. Check the card's network or BIN range configuration and verify that the app is allowlisted for Google's Push Provisioning API.

docs.title: canProvision returns a CanBeProvisioned result after the card has already been provisioned
docs.text:
If canProvision() or provisioningState() reports a previously added card as provisionable, first confirm that you are checking the same payment instrument, device, and wallet account. Re-check the state after the provisioning flow completes.

If the result remains unexpected, record the SDK result and available status code, verify the running build's allowlisting, and ask Adyen to check issuer and card-scheme configuration, including the application identifier. Do not include PAN, CVC, PIN, tokens, or opaque provisioning payloads in diagnostics.

Comparing with manual provisioning can help isolate the issue, but it is a different flow. Its behaviour alone does not prove a scheme configuration problem.

docs.title: "Something went wrong, please try again" during the provisioning flow
docs.text:
A generic Google Wallet message such as "Something went wrong, please try again" does not identify the root cause.

  1. Inspect the returned SDK result and any Google status code. Check backend failures and retain any available traceId for support.
  2. Verify package-name and signing-certificate allowlisting for the installed build.
  3. Check connectivity, Google Play services, device compatibility, and the selected wallet account.
  4. Compare with manual provisioning if supported for the card. A matching error is a useful diagnostic, not proof of a shared cause.
  5. If the issue persists, contact Adyen support with the SDK version, device/Android version, result type, status code, and, if available, trace ID. Ask for issuer and card-scheme configuration checks without sending sensitive payloads.

docs.title: Stale or destroyed Activity reference
docs.text:
Both SDKs require activityProvider to return the currently resumed Activity hosting provisioning. A lambda such as { this } or { hostActivity } captures one instance; it does not follow Activity recreation after rotation or navigation.

Neither SDK checks whether the returned Activity is finishing, destroyed, or resumed. Creation can succeed with a stale reference because the provider is called later. A destroyed Activity does not necessarily throw, so there is no guaranteed stale-Activity error result.

If the provider or provisioning UI launch throws an ordinary exception, the results are:

Operation Result Card Provisioning (Offline): provision() ProvisionResult.Failure.Other(error) Card Provisioning Sessions: provisionCard() ProvisionResult.Failure.ProvisioningFailed(message)

The SDK also uses the provider when first creating its Google Tap and Pay client. An ordinary exception there becomes CanProvisionResult.CannotBeProvisioned.Error(throwable) during canProvision(), or ProvisioningState.CannotProvision.ProvisioningFailed(message) during provisioningState(). Coroutine cancellation propagates rather than becoming a failure result.

Keep Activity-scoped SDK instances with their host and recreate them when the host is recreated. For longer-lived instances, use a lifecycle-aware provider that resolves the current provisioning host and clears it when that host pauses or is destroyed. Start operations only while the host is resumed; do not use SDK results as lifecycle checks.

See Lifecycle guidance for a provider example that applies to both SDKs.

docs.title: Tamper detection (TamperError) — Card Provisioning Sessions only
docs.text:
The Card Provisioning Sessions SDK performs Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) checks at sensitive call sites. When a threat is detected (root, hooking, memory scanning, emulator, virtual environment, compromised hardware, or a debugger attached to a release build), the SDK halts sensitive work on the client side and returns a TamperError result.

Treat a TamperError as a signal to invalidate the user's session on your backend so the session token is refused regardless of what the compromised client does next, and surface a neutral error in the UI without hinting at the reason. The full rationale and an end-to-end example are covered in the Security Guide → Respond to Tamper Signals.

If a TamperError occurs unexpectedly on a device you believe is operating normally, contact Adyen Support with the SDK version, device model, Android version, affected operation, and tamperCode. This helps us investigate possible false positives and improve detection where appropriate. Continue to treat the result as a security signal; keep the code and suspected reason out of user-facing messages.

docs.title: Card Provisioning (Offline)
docs.text: Integrate Adyen payment card provisioning into Google Wallet from your Android application.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The offline provisioning SDK adds payment cards issued through Adyen to Google Wallet directly from your app. It handles the end-to-end provisioning flow — eligibility checks, opaque payment data exchange with Google's Push Provisioning API, and reporting the final state back to your app.

“Offline” means the SDK does not call Adyen directly; your backend handles those calls. Provisioning still requires an internet connection. The Maven artifact remains provisioning-sdk, and the SDK entry point remains CardProvisioning.

The integration unfolds in four steps: your backend fetches activation data, the SDK is initialised against that data, eligibility is checked, and the card is provisioned (with an in-flight callback that lets the SDK fetch the card data via your backend).

sequenceDiagram
    box MOBILE DEVICE
        participant APP
        participant SDK
    end

    box SERVER SIDE
        participant BACKEND
        participant ADYEN
    end

    Note over APP,ADYEN: Step 1 — Get Activation Data
    APP->>BACKEND: Get Card Activation Data
    activate BACKEND
    BACKEND->>ADYEN: GET /paymentInstruments/{paymentInstrumentId}/networkTokenActivationData
    activate ADYEN
    ADYEN-->>BACKEND: sdkInput
    deactivate ADYEN
    BACKEND-->>APP: sdkInput
    deactivate BACKEND

    Note over APP,SDK: Step 2 — Initialize Provisioning Client
    APP->>SDK: CardProvisioning.create(sdkInput, activityProvider)
    SDK-->>APP: CardProvisioningCreateResult.Success(cardProvisioning)

    Note over APP,SDK: Step 3 — Check if Can Add to Wallet
    APP->>SDK: canProvision()
    SDK-->>APP: CanBeProvisioned

    Note over APP,ADYEN: Step 4 — Provision the Card
    APP->>SDK: provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider)
    activate SDK

    Note right of SDK: Callback initiated by SDK
    SDK->>APP: opcProvider.fetchOpc(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput)
    activate APP
    APP->>BACKEND: Fetch OPC(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput)
    activate BACKEND
    BACKEND->>ADYEN: POST /paymentInstruments/{paymentInstrumentId}/networkTokenActivationData with sdkOutput
    ADYEN-->>BACKEND: sdkInput (opaque OPC response)
    BACKEND-->>APP: OPC string
    deactivate BACKEND
    APP-->>SDK: OPC string
    deactivate APP

    SDK-->>APP: ProvisionResult.Success
    deactivate SDK

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Release history for the offline provisioning SDK.

This page is the canonical home for SDK release notes. The in-repo provisioning/sdk/RELEASE_NOTES flat file is generated from the latest ## VERSION section below by the :provisioning:sdk:generateModuleReleaseNotes Gradle task, and is what the GitHub + GitLab release pipelines post as the release body when a new version is cut. Add a new ## VERSION section above the previous one when releasing.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Breaking: provisioning now uses Google's Unified Push Provisioning (UPP) API, which can save a card to the user's Google account rather than only to the device that ran the provisioning flow. UPP creates the Opaque Payment Card data during the provisioning flow via the OpcProvider callback, so neither half of the deprecated pre-0.4.0 sequence can be honoured any longer: the sdkOutput is now built mid-flow, together with the session id and ephemeral key pair that only exist at that point, so one issued ahead of the flow could not be used. Both halves have therefore been removed rather than left in place to fail at runtime — see Removed below. Migrate to provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider) — see Migrating from SDK versions prior to 0.4.0.
  • OpcProvider.fetchOpc is now bounded by a 20-second timeout. A provider that does not return within that budget fails with ProvisionResult.Failure.OpcFetchError rather than leaving the Tap and Pay SDK waiting indefinitely, so an unresponsive backend no longer wedges the provisioning flow.
  • ApiException failures raised while provisioning now map onto the structured ProvisionResult.Failure variants instead of the catch-all ProvisionResult.Failure.Other.
  • Updated the SDK's bundled Google Play services Tap and Pay library (com.google.android.gms:play-services-tapandpay) to 18.10.0. The published provisioning-sdk artifact includes this library, so integrations no longer need to obtain or host it themselves. Remove any direct dependency unless another part of your app uses it. Google allowlisting is still required. Existing allowlisting for Google's legacy Tap and Pay push-provisioning API does not carry over to Unified Push Provisioning (UPP). If your app was previously approved for the legacy API, request allowlisting again for UPP before using SDK version 0.6.0 or later.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• Breaking: the pre-0.4.0 provisioning entry points, deprecated since 0.4.0, are gone. Integrations still relying on them get a compile error rather than a provisioning flow that fails on a user's device:
    • CardProvisioning.provision(sdkInput, cardDisplayName, cardAddress) — replaced by provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider).
    • CardProvisioning.createSdkOutput() and the CreateSdkOutputResult type — no replacement needed; provision(...) performs the equivalent step internally, at the point in the flow where Google requires it.
    • ProvisionResult.Failure.CreateSdkOutputNotCalled — the precondition it reported cannot arise now the OPC exchange is owned by the SDK.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Credential generation is no longer cancelled when the hosting Activity is recreated mid-provisioning, for example on rotation.
  • Provisioning operations are serialised across every CardProvisioning instance in the process, so a concurrent call now returns ProvisioningInProgress instead of interfering with the in-flight request.
  • CancellationException is no longer captured and reported as a failure result; cancellation propagates to the caller's coroutine scope.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Updated the Android Gradle Plugin to 9.1.0.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Fixed an issue where provisioning could fail for Mastercard cards when no wallet exists.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Added the OpcProvider interface and CardProvisioning.provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider) API.
  • Deprecated CreateSdkOutputResult, CardProvisioning.createSdkOutput(), and CardProvisioning.provision(sdkInput, cardDisplayName, cardAddress). These legacy entry points were removed in 0.6.0.
  • Updated the example app and README files for the new API.
  • Updated Google Tap and Pay SDK to 18.8.0.

The Activity returned should be the Activity which hosts the card provisioning functionality within the client application. This lambda is invoked on demand during provisioning operations (not at create() time), so it must always return the currently-resumed Activity. If the provider or Activity launch throws an ordinary exception, provisioning returns a failure such as ProvisionResult.Failure.Other; coroutine cancellation still propagates. docs.title: fetchOpc
docs.text:
[Provisioning SDK]\ abstract suspend fun fetchOpc(paymentInstrumentId: String, sdkOutput: String): String

Fetches the Opaque Payment Card (OPC) data required for push provisioning.

Called on a background dispatcher, once per provisioning attempt. Throw to fail the attempt: the exception is surfaced to the caller of provision as a ProvisionResult.Failure.

The SDK waits at most 20 seconds for this call, then fails the attempt with ProvisionResult.Failure.OpcFetchError - Google's Tap & Pay SDK is blocked on it throughout, so an unresponsive backend cannot be allowed to stall the flow. Keep any client-side timeout inside that budget.

Prefer a coroutine-aware HTTP client, whose calls are themselves suspend functions, over a blocking one. The SDK cancels this call when the budget expires, but cancellation only takes effect at a suspension point: a suspending client aborts the request and releases its connection, whereas a blocking call cannot be interrupted and runs to completion in the background with its result discarded. Blocking implementations are supported and the budget is enforced either way - the work simply outlives the attempt that needed it.

Do not retry inside this call. The sdkOutput carries a single-use ephemeral key, so re-sending it risks activating a second network token. Let the attempt fail and have the user restart provisioning.

docs.title: Return
docs.text: The Base64 encoded OPC string.

docs.text:

paymentInstrumentId identifies the card being provisioned. sdkOutput the single-use value to send to your backend.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Integrate the offline provisioning SDK into your Android application.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin:

  • Your application has a minSdk of 26 (Android 8.0) or higher.
  • Your application has a compileSdk of 36 or higher.
  • An API credential for the Configuration API with the Bank Issuing PaymentInstrument Network Token Activation Data role. Your backend uses it to call the networkTokenActivationData endpoints.
  • Your app ID is allowlisted by Google for the Push Provisioning API — see Google Push Provisioning API Access (shared across both SDKs in this family).

docs.title: Add the SDK
docs.text:
The Maven coordinates for this API are com.adyen.issuing.provisioning:provisioning-sdk. Before integrating, confirm that your intended version is listed on Maven Central. Older releases used different coordinates; do not assume they expose the API described here.

Add the dependency to your app module's build.gradle.kts:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.adyen.issuing.provisioning:provisioning-sdk:0.6.0")
}

Tip

Always check Maven Central for the latest version before integrating.

docs.title: Request Google Push Provisioning API Access
docs.text:
The SDK uses Google's Push Provisioning API (com.google.android.gms:play-services-tapandpay), and your app must be allowlisted by Google before the API accepts its calls. Allowlisting is a one-time setup that applies to either SDK in this family.

The published SDK artifact bundles the Push Provisioning API library, so there is no separate play-services-tapandpay dependency to add or host. If your build previously declared a direct dependency on it for the Adyen SDK, you can remove it — provided no other part of your app uses the library.

Follow the family-level guide: Google Push Provisioning API Access.

docs.title: Fetch Provisioning Data from Your Backend
docs.text:
Every provisioning flow begins with your backend fetching opaque sdkInput data from Adyen for a specific payment instrument.

From your backend, perform a GET request to:

Environment URL Test https://balanceplatform-api-test.adyen.com/bcl/v2/paymentInstruments/{paymentInstrumentId}/networkTokenActivationData Live https://balanceplatform-api-live.adyen.com/bcl/v2/paymentInstruments/{paymentInstrumentId}/networkTokenActivationData

Headers:

  • Content-Type: application/json
  • X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY, using the Configuration API key from your Balance Platform Customer Area

See the Configuration API reference for the full request and response contract. The later POST to the same endpoint, made from your OpcProvider, uses the same host and credential.

The response contains an sdkInput string. Your backend returns this string to your Android app.

Note

The sdkInput is opaque — your app does not need to parse or interpret it. Forward it to the SDK as-is.

docs.title: Create a Provisioning Instance
docs.text:
With sdkInput in hand, create a CardProvisioning instance by calling the static factory:

Experimental API

The CardProvisioning API is annotated @AdyenExperimentalApi and requires an explicit opt-in at each call site: annotate the calling function with @OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class) (or add @file:OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class) at the top of the file). Without it, code using the SDK does not compile.

@file:OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class)

import com.adyen.issuing.mobile.provisioning.client.annotation.AdyenExperimentalApi

val result = CardProvisioning.create(
    sdkInput = sdkInput,
    activityProvider = { cardIssuingActivity },
)

val cardProvisioning = when (result) {
    is CardProvisioningCreateResult.Success ->
        result.cardProvisioning
    is CardProvisioningCreateResult.Failed.GooglePayNotSupported -> {
        // Device does not support Google Pay; hide the "Add to Google Wallet" button
        return
    }
    is CardProvisioningCreateResult.Failed.InvalidSdkInput -> {
        // sdkInput is malformed; surface the error to your backend
        return
    }
}

The activityProvider lambda is invoked on demand — not at create() time but later, when the SDK needs to launch Google's provisioning UI (e.g. during provision() or wallet creation). It must always return the currently-resumed Activity that hosts your card-issuing UI.

docs.title: Lifecycle guidance
docs.text:
• Keep Activity-scoped instances with their host. A lambda such as { this } captures that Activity, just like { activity } captures a stored reference. Neither follows Activity recreation. Recreate the provisioning instance with its host and launch operations only while the host is resumed.
  • Resolve the host dynamically for longer-lived instances. If you retain the provisioning instance in a ViewModel or application-scoped object, use a lifecycle-aware provider that tracks the currently resumed provisioning host and clears its reference when that host pauses or is destroyed. Do not fall back to an unrelated Activity.
// currentProvisioningActivity is maintained by your app's lifecycle tracker.
val result = CardProvisioning.create(
    sdkInput = sdkInput,
    activityProvider = {
        checkNotNull(currentProvisioningActivity) { "No resumed provisioning host" }
    },
)
  • Handle launch failures and cancellation. The provider's return type is non-null Activity. If the provider or Activity launch throws an ordinary exception, provisioning maps it to a failure such as ProvisionResult.Failure.Other; coroutine cancellation still propagates. A destroyed Activity does not necessarily throw, so do not rely on the SDK to detect a stale reference.
  • Process death does not return a result. Recreate SDK instances after the app restarts and re-check provisioning state before offering a new attempt. Do not assume an interrupted flow completed or failed.

docs.title: Check Whether a Card Can Be Provisioned
docs.text:
Before showing an "Add to Google Wallet" button, ask the SDK whether the device and Google Wallet account can accept this card:

val canProvision = cardProvisioning.canProvision() == CanProvisionResult.CanBeProvisioned

canProvision() is a suspend function — call it from a coroutine. The result reflects Google Wallet's view of the device + card combination at the moment of the call; treat it as advisory and re-check if the user revisits the screen later.

Note

canProvision() returns CanBeProvisioned only when the card is eligible and not already in the wallet. If the card has already been added on this device, you will get CannotBeProvisioned.AlreadyExistsInWallet. Surface that state by hiding or replacing the "Add to Google Wallet" button rather than re-attempting provisioning.

docs.title: Add a Card to Google Wallet
docs.text: When the user taps "Add to Google Wallet", drive the provisioning flow in two parts: implement an OpcProvider that knows how to fetch Opaque Payment Card (OPC) data from your backend on demand, then call provision() with a card display label, a CardAddress, and the provider. cardDisplayName is the user-facing card label supplied to Google Wallet, not the cardholder's name.

docs.title: Implement an OpcProvider
docs.text:
The SDK calls OpcProvider.fetchOpc mid-flow once it has obtained an sdkOutput value to send to Adyen. Your implementation forwards sdkOutput to your backend, which performs a POST against /paymentInstruments/{paymentInstrumentId}/networkTokenActivationData with sdkOutput in the body, and returns the resulting OPC string back to the SDK.

val opcProvider = OpcProvider { paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput ->
    // Forward sdkOutput to your backend, which calls Adyen and returns the OPC string.
    // POST /paymentInstruments/{paymentInstrumentId}/networkTokenActivationData
    // Body: { "sdkOutput": sdkOutput }
    val opc: String = backend.fetchOpaquePaymentCard(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput)
    opc
}

fetchOpc is a suspend function, invoked on a background dispatcher. If the call fails, throw — the SDK catches the exception and surfaces it as a ProvisionResult.Failure to your caller.

fetchOpc has a 20-second budget

The Google Tap and Pay SDK cannot complete its request until your fetchOpc callback returns. If fetchOpc has not returned within 20 seconds, the Adyen provisioning SDK stops waiting and fails the attempt with ProvisionResult.Failure.OpcFetchError.

Set your own client timeouts comfortably inside that budget. Do not retry inside fetchOpc — the sdkOutput is single-use, so re-sending it risks a second network-token activation. Let the call fail and have the user retry the whole flow.

Use a coroutine-aware HTTP client

Prefer an HTTP client that provides suspend functions, for example Retrofit or Ktor, rather than a blocking client.

When the budget expires the SDK cancels your call, but cancellation can only take effect at a suspension point. A suspending client acts on it: the request is aborted and its connection released. A blocking call — execute(), Thread.sleep, runBlocking — cannot be interrupted, so it runs to completion in the background holding a thread, with its result discarded. Blocking calls remain supported and the 20-second budget is enforced either way; they simply cannot be cancelled, so the work outlives the attempt that needed it.

docs.title: Call provision()
docs.text:
val result = cardProvisioning.provision(
    cardDisplayName = "Adyen Business Card",
    cardAddress = CardAddress(),
    opcProvider = opcProvider,
)

when (result) {
    is ProvisionResult.Success -> handleProvisioningSuccess(result.tokenId)
    // The user closed Google's flow. This is not an error, so leave the UI unchanged.
    ProvisionResult.Failure.Canceled -> Unit
    is ProvisionResult.Failure -> handleProvisioningFailure(result)
}

provision() is a suspend function and presents Google's native "Add to Wallet" UI as part of its execution; call it from the Activity lifecycle (e.g. inside a lifecycleScope.launch { ... } triggered by the user's button tap).

Canceled means the user closed Google's provisioning flow. Nothing was added to the wallet and nothing failed, so do not show an error message. For other failures, log the result type for diagnostics and show the cardholder your own text. The error strings some variants carry are in English, are not localized, and are not meant for display.

Note

Passing an empty CardAddress() defers the address-entry step to Google Wallet's native flow — the user will be prompted to enter their address during provisioning. If you already have a verified address for the cardholder, populate the CardAddress fields to skip that step.

docs.title: Migrating from SDK versions prior to 0.4.0
docs.text:
Guidance for upgrading existing integrations from provisioning-sdk 0.3.x and earlier to 0.6.0+, which is built on Google's Unified Push Provisioning.

Migrating straight to Card Provisioning Sessions?

If you are on < 0.4.0 and your end goal is the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK, you can skip this migration entirely. The Card Provisioning Sessions SDK uses provisioning-sdk internally and exposes a different client API — the createSdkOutput() / OpcProvider / direct-SDK distinctions never surface in your code. Follow the getting started guide for the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK instead. This page is for integrations that intend to stay on the offline provisioning SDK.

docs.title: Why upgrade
docs.text:
The primary reason to move to 0.6.0+ is support for Google's Unified Push Provisioning (UPP).

Every release up to and including the 0.4.x line is built on Google's legacy Tap and Pay push-provisioning API. Google has deprecated that API and replaced it with Unified Push Provisioning, which can save a card to the user's Google account rather than only to the specific device that ran the provisioning flow. 0.6.0 is the first release built on UPP.

How much work the upgrade involves depends on where you are starting from:

  • Already on 0.4.x — you are on the current client API, so no call signatures need to change. Update the dependency version and add @OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class) at affected CardProvisioning call sites if you have not already opted in. Skip to step 4.
  • On < 0.4.0 — you have a breaking-change API migration to do as well as the version bump, because the pre-0.4.0 createSdkOutput() + provision(sdkInput, …) API cannot be preserved on top of UPP. That migration is the subject of this page.

The current API is built around a single OpcProvider callback that the SDK invokes when it requires the Opaque Payment Card (OPC) data, rather than requiring the application to orchestrate that exchange. Pre-0.4.0 integrations call createSdkOutput(), send the resulting sdkOutput to the backend to retrieve the OPC value from Adyen, and only then call provision(sdkInput, cardDisplayName, cardAddress). From 0.4.0 you pass an OpcProvider to a single provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider) call, and the SDK performs the round-trip internally.

Secondary benefits picked up along the way:

  • Fewer steps at the call site. One provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider) call replaces the two-stage createSdkOutput → backend call → provision(sdkInput, …) sequence.
  • Backend integration is unchanged. The two networkTokenActivationData endpoints (GET for sdkInput, POST for OPC) still carry the same payloads — only the timing of their invocation from the client changes.
  • Unified error handling. Failures inside the OPC retrieval surface through the single ProvisionResult returned from the new overload, rather than being split across CreateSdkOutputResult and ProvisionResult.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
Both pre-0.4.0 entry points were deprecated in 0.4.0 and are removed in 0.6.0. They are the two halves of one legacy sequence, so neither survives on its own.

Code still calling them stops compiling, on purpose. Because 0.6.0+ is built on Google's Unified Push Provisioning API, the Opaque Payment Card is created during the provisioning flow rather than supplied up-front, so the sdkInput parameter of the old provision(...) overload has nothing left to carry. sdkOutput cannot be pre-built either: it bundles values that first exist mid-flow — the session id Google supplies, and the single-use ephemeral key your backend's response is encrypted to. An sdkOutput obtained ahead of the flow would carry no session id, so your backend would not create a Google Opaque Payment Card for it. Nothing would be able to decrypt the response either — exchanging it with your backend could only waste a network-token activation. The old calls are therefore removed rather than left to fail at runtime: your build stops at exactly the call sites that need migrating, instead of shipping a provisioning flow that fails on a user's device.

API Status Replacement CardProvisioning.createSdkOutput(): CreateSdkOutputResult @Deprecated in 0.4.0; removed in 0.6.0 Not needed — the new provision(...) overload performs the equivalent step internally, at the point in the flow where Google requires it. CardProvisioning.provision(sdkInput, cardDisplayName, cardAddress): ProvisionResult @Deprecated in 0.4.0; removed in 0.6.0 provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider): ProvisionResult CreateSdkOutputResult (sealed interface and all Success / Failure.* variants) @Deprecated in 0.4.0; removed in 0.6.0 Failure cases that previously surfaced here now flow through ProvisionResult.Failure. ProvisionResult.Failure.CreateSdkOutputNotCalled @Deprecated in 0.4.0; removed in 0.6.0 No replacement — the precondition it reported cannot arise once the OPC exchange is owned by the SDK.

Migrating to provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider) also means supplying an OpcProvider implementation that performs the OPC backend call your own code used to orchestrate.

docs.title: OpcProvider interface
docs.text:
OpcProvider is a fun interface (single abstract method, so it accepts a SAM lambda):

public fun interface OpcProvider {
    public suspend fun fetchOpc(
        paymentInstrumentId: String,
        sdkOutput: String,
    ): String
}

The SDK invokes fetchOpc once per provision(...) call, passing the paymentInstrumentId of the card being provisioned and a newly issued sdkOutput. The implementation must return the base64-encoded OPC string from the backend. Exceptions thrown from fetchOpc propagate as a ProvisionResult.Failure, allowing retries and error mapping to be handled alongside the rest of the provisioning error handling.

Unlike the pre-0.4.0 sequence — where the backend call sat in your own code and could take as long as you allowed — fetchOpc runs inside Google's provisioning flow and is bounded by a 20-second timeout, after which the attempt fails with ProvisionResult.Failure.OpcFetchError. Code moved out of the old two-stage sequence should have its client timeouts checked against that budget.

fetchOpc is a suspend function, so this is also a good opportunity to move the call onto a coroutine-aware HTTP client if it was previously blocking. The SDK cancels the call when the budget expires, but only a suspending client can act on that and abort the request — a blocking call runs to completion in the background with its result discarded.

docs.title: 1. Replace createSdkOutput() callers with an OpcProvider
docs.text:
Anywhere the OPC round-trip was previously invoked manually:

val sdkOutputResult = cardProvisioning.createSdkOutput()
val sdkOutput = (sdkOutputResult as CreateSdkOutputResult.Success).sdkOutput
val opc = backend.requestOpaquePaymentCardData(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput).sdkInput

…relocate the same backend call into a lambda that the SDK invokes on your behalf:

val opcProvider = OpcProvider { paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput ->
    backend.requestOpaquePaymentCardData(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput).sdkInput
}

If OpcProvider is the only argument requiring SAM conversion at the call site, it can also be inlined as a named lambda — see step 2.

docs.title: 2. Update the provision(...) call site
docs.text:
Before — pre-0.4.0 sequence with the backend exchange in client code:

// 1. Request sdkOutput from the SDK.
val sdkOutputResult = cardProvisioning.createSdkOutput()
val sdkOutput = (sdkOutputResult as CreateSdkOutputResult.Success).sdkOutput

// 2. Call the backend to exchange sdkOutput for the card data.
val opc = backend.requestOpaquePaymentCardData(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput).sdkInput

// 3. Pass the card data back to the SDK to complete provisioning.
val provisionResult = cardProvisioning.provision(
    sdkInput = opc,
    cardDisplayName = "Adyen Business Card",
    cardAddress = CardAddress(),
)

After — single call with an OpcProvider:

@OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class)
val provisionResult = cardProvisioning.provision(
    cardDisplayName = "Adyen Business Card",
    cardAddress = CardAddress(),
    opcProvider = { paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput ->
        backend.requestOpaquePaymentCardData(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput).sdkInput
    },
)

Like every CardProvisioning call site, the provision(...) call needs the @OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class) opt-in shown above — see Getting Started.

The example app's ProvisioningSdkRepository demonstrates the same pattern integrated with a real backend client.

docs.title: 3. Remove the now-unused CreateSdkOutputResult handling
docs.text: Any when expression that exhausted CreateSdkOutputResult.Success / CreateSdkOutputResult.Failure.* branches must be removed — the type no longer exists in 0.6.0. Failures that previously surfaced there are now reflected in the ProvisionResult returned by the new provision(...) — update the existing ProvisionResult mapping if it does not already cover those cases. A when over ProvisionResult.Failure that branched on CreateSdkOutputNotCalled needs that branch dropped for the same reason.

docs.title: 4. Update the dependency version
docs.text:
Move to 0.6.0 or later — earlier releases are built on the legacy Tap and Pay API and do not include the UPP implementation. Update the published version in the module's build.gradle.kts:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.adyen.issuing.provisioning:provisioning-sdk:0.6.0")
}

Bumping to 0.6.0+ also changes how Google's Push Provisioning API library reaches your build: the published provisioning-sdk artifact now bundles play-services-tapandpay. If you previously obtained the artifact from Google and hosted it in your local Maven cache or an internal repository for the SDK, you can remove that direct dependency — provided no other part of your app uses the library. The hosting setup is no longer needed for the SDK, but your app must still be allowlisted by Google — see Google Push Provisioning API Access.

Upgrading from legacy Tap and Pay

Existing allowlisting for Google's legacy Tap and Pay push-provisioning API does not carry over to Unified Push Provisioning (UPP). If your app was previously approved for the legacy API, request allowlisting again for UPP before using SDK version 0.6.0 or later.

docs.text:
• CardProvisioning.create(sdkInput, activityProvider) — unchanged. The sdkInput returned by the GET /networkTokenActivationData backend call is still passed at construction time.
  • canProvision() — unchanged signature and CanProvisionResult variants.
  • CardAddress — same package, same fields.
  • Backend endpoints — the two networkTokenActivationData calls are still issued; only the timing of their invocation on the client changes.

docs.title: Card Provisioning Sessions
docs.text: Add Adyen-issued payment cards to Google Wallet through a session-based integration.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Card Provisioning Sessions SDK wraps the same Google Push Provisioning flow as the offline provisioning SDK, but mediates the back-and-forth with Adyen behind a session token. Your backend obtains a session token via Adyen's session API and hands it to the SDK; the SDK then drives the entire provisioning flow without further backend involvement per step.

The result is a smaller backend surface area and a simpler client integration — at the cost of being slightly less flexible than the offline provisioning SDK if you need step-by-step control.

The integration unfolds in three steps: your backend obtains session tokens on demand, the card's provisioning state is checked through the session, and the cardholder adds the card to Google Wallet. The SDK handles the rest of the protocol with Adyen behind the scenes.

sequenceDiagram
    box MOBILE DEVICE
        participant APP
        participant SDK
    end

    box SERVER SIDE
        participant BACKEND
        participant ADYEN
    end

    Note over APP,ADYEN: Step 1 — Get Session Token
    APP->>BACKEND: Request Session Token
    activate BACKEND
    BACKEND->>ADYEN: Request Session Token
    activate ADYEN
    ADYEN-->>BACKEND: Return Session Token
    deactivate ADYEN
    BACKEND-->>APP: Return Session Token
    deactivate BACKEND

    Note over APP,SDK: Step 2 — Check Provisioning State
    APP->>SDK: provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId)
    activate SDK
    SDK-->>APP: ProvisioningState.CanProvision
    deactivate SDK

    Note over APP,SDK: Step 3 — Provision the Card
    APP->>SDK: provisionCard(paymentInstrumentId, ...)
    activate SDK
    SDK-->>APP: ProvisionResult.Success
    deactivate SDK

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Session-based card provisioning to Google Wallet using Google's Unified Push Provisioning (UPP) API through provisioning-sdk 0.6.0.
  • Session creation with ProvisioningSessionConfiguration containing DER-encoded application certificate bytes, payment instrument IDs, and a SessionEnvironment (Live or Test). A SessionTokenProvider supplies fresh backend tokens wrapped in an opaque SessionToken.
  • provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId) reports CanProvision, Provisioned, or CannotProvision. provisionCard handles the activation-data exchange and wallet provisioning flow without a per-step OPC callback.
  • Structured creation and operation results through ProvisioningSessionCreateResult, ProvisioningState, and ProvisionResult. Backend-related failures expose an optional traceId for support correlation.
  • Runtime tamper detection returns TamperError results. Integrations must invalidate the user's session on their backend when these occur.

See Getting Started for integration guidance, or Migrating from provisioning-sdk to upgrade an existing direct SDK integration.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Integrate the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK into your Android application.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin:

  • Your application has a minSdk of 26 (Android 8.0) or higher.
  • Your application has a compileSdk of 36 or higher.
  • An API credential with the Network Token: Create role.
  • Your app ID is allowlisted by Google for the Push Provisioning API — see Google Push Provisioning API Access (shared across both SDKs in this family).

In addition, the Session-based SDK requires an application certificate provided by Adyen — see below.

docs.title: Card Provisioning Sessions application certificate
docs.text:
The application certificate is specific to your application and lets the SDK verify the host application at runtime. You can request it from your Adyen Project Operations Manager or Implementation Manager. You will need to provide your Android application's applicationId (look for the applicationId property in your main app module's build.gradle.kts).

If your applicationId ever changes, request a new certificate for the new id — the existing one will not match.

The certificate is provided as a file with a .cer extension. You will embed it in your app in step 1.

docs.title: 1. Embed the Certificate
docs.text:
Add the .cer file Adyen provided to your app module's res/raw resource directory (create it if you do not already have one). At runtime, load its DER-encoded bytes:

// Load the DER-encoded certificate bytes from a raw resource named `app_cert`.
val appCertificate: ByteArray =
    context.resources.openRawResource(R.raw.app_cert).use { it.readBytes() }

You will pass these bytes to ProvisioningSession.create() in step 4.

docs.title: 2. Fetch a Session Token
docs.text:
Each provisioning attempt is scoped to a session token your backend obtains from the Adyen API. From your backend, perform:

URL — https://authe-live.adyen.com/authe/api/v1/sessions (live) or https://test.adyen.com/authe/api/v1/sessions (test) — use the corresponding host for your target environment (see Environments).

Headers

  • Content-Type: application/json
  • X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY

Body

{
    "product": "platform",
    "policy": {
        "resources": [
            { "type": "paymentInstrument", "paymentInstrumentId": "PI..." }
        ],
        "roles": ["Network Token: Create"]
    }
}

Have your backend return the resulting session token to your Android app on demand. The SDK will request a token via the SessionTokenProvider callback you provide in step 4.

Return a fresh token on every provider invocation; do not cache or reuse tokens. If the provider throws, the SDK retries retrieval up to two times (three invocations in total). A returned token that fails local validation is not retried.

See the session authentication API reference for the full request and response contract.

docs.title: 3. Add Card Provisioning Sessions Dependency
docs.text:
Add the dependency to your app module's build.gradle.kts:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.adyen.issuing.provisioning:provisioning-sessions:0.6.0")
}

Or the equivalent version catalog entry.

Tip

Always check Maven Central for the latest version before integrating.

docs.title: 4. Initialize the Provisioning Session
docs.text:
Create a ProvisioningSession via the static factory:

public fun create(
    context: Context,
    configuration: ProvisioningSessionConfiguration,
    activityProvider: () -> Activity,
    tokenProvider: SessionTokenProvider
): ProvisioningSessionCreateResult

Experimental API

The Sessions SDK public API is annotated @AdyenExperimentalApi and requires an explicit opt-in at each call site: annotate the calling function with @OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class) (or add @file:OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class) at the top of the file). Without it, code using the SDK does not compile.

Parameter rundown:

  • context — pass context.applicationContext. Use an application-scoped context, not an Activity, so the session is not tied to an Activity lifecycle.
  • configuration — a ProvisioningSessionConfiguration bundling:
    • appCertificate — the DER-encoded certificate bytes from step 1.
    • paymentInstrumentIds — the payment instruments that may be provisioned during this session.
    • environment — defaults to SessionEnvironment.Live. See Environments.
  • activityProvider — function returning the host Activity (typically the Activity hosting your card-provisioning screen, or your single-Activity app's main Activity). This lambda is invoked on demand when the SDK needs to launch Google's provisioning UI — not at create() time. It must always return the currently-resumed Activity. Do not return a destroyed Activity or retain a captured Activity beyond its lifecycle. Exceptions from the provider or launch are mapped to failures; coroutine cancellation still propagates. See the Provisioning SDK lifecycle guidance for recommended patterns — the same rules apply here.
  • tokenProvider — the SessionTokenProvider the SDK invokes when it needs a session token (see step 2). It is a fun interface, so a lambda works: return the token your backend fetched, wrapped in a SessionToken.

Note

The SDK parses the DER certificate bytes inside ProvisioningSession.create(). If they cannot be parsed as X.509, the result is ProvisioningSessionCreateResult.Failure.ApplicationCertificateError. SessionToken is an opaque wrapper — its constructor is public so you can wrap the raw token your backend returns, but the wrapped value is internal to the SDK, keeping the token out of your logs and crash reports.

The following wiring is illustrative: httpClient, request/response helpers, backend URLs, and UI functions are application-defined pseudocode, not a runnable HTTP-client implementation. Use an authenticated HTTPS endpoint on your own backend and adapt the response parsing to its contract.

@file:OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class)

import com.adyen.issuing.mobile.provisioning.client.annotation.AdyenExperimentalApi

suspend fun fetchSessionTokenFromBackend(paymentInstrumentIds: Set<String>): String {
    val body = buildSessionTokenRequestBody(paymentInstrumentIds) // see step 2
    val response = httpClient.post("yourBackend/sessionToken", body)
    if (!response.isSuccessful()) {
        // Throw — the SDK will surface the failure as a Failure result to your caller.
        throw IllegalStateException("Could not fetch session token: ${response.code}")
    }
    return response.bodyText()
}

val result = ProvisioningSession.create(
    context = applicationContext,
    configuration = ProvisioningSessionConfiguration(
        appCertificate = appCertificate,
        paymentInstrumentIds = setOf("PI...01", "PI...02")
    ),
    activityProvider = { provisioningActivity },
    tokenProvider = { paymentInstrumentIds ->
        SessionToken(fetchSessionTokenFromBackend(paymentInstrumentIds))
    },
)

val provisioningSession = when (result) {
    is ProvisioningSessionCreateResult.Success ->
        result.session
    is ProvisioningSessionCreateResult.Failure.ApplicationCertificateError ->
        throw IllegalStateException("Invalid application certificate")
    is ProvisioningSessionCreateResult.Failure.Error ->
        throw IllegalStateException("Unexpected initialization error: ${result.message}")
}

The Failure variants distinguish between a malformed / mis-issued application certificate and any other unexpected initialization error.

docs.title: 5. Check the Card's Provisioning State
docs.text:
Before showing an "Add to Google Wallet" button, ask the session whether each card can be added to the user's wallet:

when (val result = provisioningSession.provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId)) {
    // Card is ready to be added to the wallet.
    ProvisioningState.CanProvision ->
        showAddToWalletButton()
    // Card has already been added to this device's wallet — a positive state.
    ProvisioningState.Provisioned ->
        hideAddToWalletButton()
    // Card cannot be added for some other reason.
    is ProvisioningState.CannotProvision ->
        showCannotProvisionReason(result)
}

provisioningState() is a suspend function — call it from a coroutine. Treat the result as advisory and re-check if the user revisits the screen later.

ProvisioningState.CannotProvision reports why the card cannot be added — from backend problems (HttpError, CouldNotEstablishSession, ActivationDataUnavailable) through wallet support (WalletNotSupported) to RASP violations (TamperError, covered in step 8). The backend-related variants carry a traceId correlation id — see step 7.

docs.title: 6. Add the Card to Google Wallet
docs.text:
When the user taps "Add to Google Wallet", drive Google's native provisioning flow. cardDisplayName is the user-facing card label supplied to Google Wallet, not the cardholder's name:

val provisionResult = provisioningSession.provisionCard(
    paymentInstrumentId = paymentInstrumentId,
    cardDisplayName = "Adyen Business Card",
    cardAddress = CardAddress(),
)

provisionCard() is a suspend function and presents Google's native "Add to Wallet" UI as part of its execution. Call it from the Activity lifecycle (e.g. inside lifecycleScope.launch { ... } triggered by the user's tap).

Note

Passing an empty CardAddress() defers the address-entry step to Google Wallet's native flow — the user will be prompted to enter their address during provisioning. If you already have a verified address for the cardholder, populate the CardAddress fields to skip that step.

docs.title: 7. Handle the Final State
docs.text:
provisionCard() returns a ProvisionResult once the Google Wallet flow completes (successfully or otherwise). Branch on it to update your UI:

when (provisionResult) {
    is ProvisionResult.Success ->
        handleProvisioningSuccess(provisionResult.tokenId)
    // The user closed Google's flow. This is not an error, so leave the UI unchanged.
    ProvisionResult.Failure.ProvisioningCancelled ->
        Unit
    is ProvisionResult.Failure ->
        handleProvisioningFailure(provisionResult)
}

The Failure hierarchy distinguishes error categories such as user cancellation (ProvisioningCancelled), another provisioning or wallet-creation operation running in the application process, possibly for another card (ProvisioningAlreadyInProgress), session and backend problems (SessionTokenRetrievalFailed, CouldNotEstablishSession, ActivationDataUnavailable, HttpError), and the tamper signal covered next.

CouldNotEstablishSession, ActivationDataUnavailable, and HttpError include an optional traceId. Share it with Adyen support to help locate the failed backend request. It comes from the response's traceparent header and is null if that header is missing or invalid.

HttpError has three variants:

Variant HTTP status message Authentication 401 or 403 Decrypted backend error text, or null if unavailable Validation 422 Decrypted backend error text, or null if unavailable Server 500 or any other unexpected non-2xx status Fixed support guidance, not backend error text

Server.message is "Contact Adyen Support" for HTTP 500, or "Contact Adyen Support unexpected response code: {httpCode}" otherwise. There is no separate HTTP-code property.

docs.title: Treat cancellation as a normal outcome
docs.text: ProvisioningCancelled means the user closed Google's provisioning flow. Nothing was added to the wallet and nothing failed, so leave your UI as it was. Do not show an error message.

docs.title: Write your own text for the cardholder
docs.text: Log failures for diagnostics, including the result type and any traceId. For anything the cardholder sees, map the result type to your own text. The message values are not meant for display: they are in English and are not localized, and HttpError.Server.message is guidance for you to contact Adyen support, not something to show a cardholder.

docs.title: 8. Respond to TamperError
docs.text:
Both provisioningState() and provisionCard() may return a TamperError variant when the SDK's Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) checks detect that the device has been compromised — root, hooking, memory scanning, emulator, virtual environment, compromised hardware, or a debugger attached to a release build.

When you receive a TamperError, treat it as a signal to invalidate the user's session on your backend. The SDK halts sensitive work on the client side, but it does not terminate the server-side session — that responsibility is delegated to you so the response composes with your wider fraud controls.

when (val result = provisioningSession.provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId)) {
    is ProvisioningState.CannotProvision.TamperError -> {
        // Revoke the session on your backend so the session token is refused
        // regardless of what the compromised client does next, then surface a
        // neutral error to the user.
        backend.invalidateSession()
        showGenericErrorAndLogOut()
    }
    // … handle other result variants
    else -> { /* … */ }
}

when (val result = provisioningSession.provisionCard(paymentInstrumentId, cardDisplayName, cardAddress)) {
    is ProvisionResult.Failure.TamperError -> {
        backend.invalidateSession()
        showGenericErrorAndLogOut()
    }
    // … handle other result variants
    else -> { /* … */ }
}

Do not surface the specific tamper reason to the user — a neutral error message avoids giving attackers feedback on which check triggered. The tamperCode on the result is intended for reporting to Adyen support, not for end-user display.

See Respond to Tamper Signals in the Security Guide for the full rationale, including why the client-side SDK does not self-wipe keys or cached state on detection.

docs.title: Migrating from Card Provisioning (Offline) to Card Provisioning Sessions
docs.text:
Guidance for moving an existing integration from the offline provisioning SDK to the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK.

The example app contains both integrations side-by-side under provisioningsdk/ and provisioningsessions/, sharing a single ProvisioningRepository interface — a useful concrete reference for the diff described below.

Coming from a < 0.4.0 Card Provisioning (Offline)?

You don't need to do the pre-0.4 migration first. The "Before" snippets on this page show the offline provisioning SDK API from 0.4.0 onward so the diff to the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK is small, but if your existing integration is on < 0.4.0 you can replace it with the Session-based flow directly — none of the pre-0.4.0 createSdkOutput() / manual OPC orchestration carries over either way. Use the getting started guide for the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK as your primary reference and treat the "Before" snippets here as illustrative of what an offline provisioning SDK call site looks like, not as a prerequisite your code must already match.

docs.title: Why migrate
docs.text:
Session-based provisioning consolidates several integration concerns that the offline provisioning SDK delegates to the backend:

  • Smaller backend surface area. A single session-token endpoint replaces the two-leg networkTokenActivationData exchange (GET for sdkInput, POST with sdkOutput for OPC). Once the session token is issued, the SDK handles the remainder of the provisioning protocol with Adyen internally.
  • Multi-card sessions. A single ProvisioningSession covers a Set<String> of payment-instrument IDs, so flows that present several cards at once (e.g. a wallet management screen) incur the session-creation cost only once.
  • Tamper-detection signals. The session pipeline surfaces device-tamper outcomes alongside the standard provisioning results, providing an integrated signal in client error handling rather than a separate workflow.
  • Simpler client lifecycle. No OpcProvider callback to integrate with the backend; no per-step opaque-payload handling in application code.

The trade-off is reduced step-by-step control. If there are integration-specific reasons to stage sdkInput / sdkOutput through application logic between canProvision and provision, the offline provisioning SDK remains the appropriate choice.

docs.title: Flow comparison
docs.text: The diagrams below compare the two integrations. With Sessions, your backend provides a session token and the SDK handles the remaining communication with Adyen. Your app no longer needs an OPC callback during provisioning.

docs.title: Card Provisioning (Offline) — four-step flow with OPC callback

sequenceDiagram

        participant APP

        participant BACKEND
        participant ADYEN
