docs.title: API mapping
docs.text:
Concern Card Provisioning (Offline) Card Provisioning Sessions Maven coordinate com.adyen.issuing.provisioning:provisioning-sdk com.adyen.issuing.provisioning:provisioning-sessions Primary type CardProvisioning (one instance per card) ProvisioningSession (one instance per card set) Factory CardProvisioning.create(sdkInput, activityProvider) ProvisioningSession.create(context, configuration, activityProvider, tokenProvider) Configuration (none) ProvisioningSessionConfiguration(appCertificate: ByteArray, paymentInstrumentIds, environment = SessionEnvironment.Live) Eligibility check canProvision(): CanProvisionResult provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId): ProvisioningState Provision provision(cardDisplayName, cardAddress, opcProvider): ProvisionResult provisionCard(paymentInstrumentId, cardDisplayName, cardAddress): ProvisionResult Backend bridge OpcProvider lambda fetches OPC per call SessionTokenProvider returns a session token wrapped in SessionToken Application certificate Not required Required — DER-encoded bytes in ProvisioningSessionConfiguration Environment selector Not exposed SessionEnvironment (Live or Test) Result types package com.adyen.issuing.mobile.provisioning.client.results.* com.adyen.issuing.mobile.provisioning.sessions.results.* Card address type com.adyen.issuing.mobile.provisioning.client.data.CardAddress Same type, re-used across both SDKs Activity provider () -> Activity Same signature Experimental opt-in @AdyenExperimentalApi Same annotation

The two SDKs use distinct results packages with different concrete variants, so any when expression that is exhaustive over the SDK's CanProvisionResult / ProvisionResult / CardProvisioningCreateResult branches will need to be updated to cover the Sessions counterparts (ProvisioningState, ProvisionResult, ProvisioningSessionCreateResult). See Result-type changes below.

docs.title: What goes away
docs.text:
The two networkTokenActivationData calls used by the direct SDK are no longer invoked from the client:

  • GET .../paymentInstruments/{id}/networkTokenActivationData — previously returned sdkInput.
  • POST .../paymentInstruments/{id}/networkTokenActivationData — previously returned the OPC payload in exchange for sdkOutput.

Once no consumers of the offline provisioning SDK remain, the corresponding backend endpoints can be decommissioned.

docs.title: What replaces them
docs.text:
A single endpoint on your backend that creates an Adyen session token for the set of payment-instrument IDs the user is about to operate on. Its response — the session token issued by Adyen's session API — is what your SessionTokenProvider returns to the SDK, wrapped in the SDK's opaque SessionToken type.

The provider is a fun interface, so a lambda works:

tokenProvider = { paymentInstrumentIds ->
    // Single backend call: the endpoint requests a token from Adyen's session API
    SessionToken(sessionsBackend.fetchToken(paymentInstrumentIds))
}

It receives the same paymentInstrumentIds set you passed in ProvisioningSessionConfiguration and must return the session token wrapped in a SessionToken. The token must carry the Network Token: Create role and cover the session's payment instruments; the SDK validates these claims locally before use.

Your backend obtains the token by calling Adyen's session API:

  • Live — POST https://authe-live.adyen.com/authe/api/v1/sessions
  • Test — POST https://test.adyen.com/authe/api/v1/sessions

The POST returns:

{
    "id": "SESSION_ID...",
    "token": "SESSION_TOKEN..."
}

The token is the value your tokenProvider lambda returns to the SDK; the id is informational and can help with debugging on the backend side. Request a fresh token each time the SDK invokes your tokenProvider; do not cache or reuse tokens. If the provider throws, the SDK retries token retrieval up to two times (three invocations in total). A token that returns successfully but fails local validation is not retried. Do not assume the provider runs only once per session or operation.

For the full request and response contract, see the session authentication API reference.

docs.title: Client code changes
docs.text: The example app demonstrates both call sequences side-by-side; the snippets below summarise the differences.

docs.title: Before — Card Provisioning (Offline)
docs.text:
// Backend call 1: GET networkTokenActivationData -> sdkInput
val sdkInput: String = sdkBackend.requestCardActivation(paymentInstrumentId).sdkInput

val createResult = CardProvisioning.create(
    sdkInput = sdkInput,
    activityProvider = { hostingActivity },
)
val cardProvisioning = (createResult as CardProvisioningCreateResult.Success).cardProvisioning

when (cardProvisioning.canProvision()) {
    is CanProvisionResult.CanBeProvisioned -> { /* show Add to Wallet */ }
    is CanProvisionResult.CannotBeProvisioned.AlreadyExistsInWallet -> { /* hide button */ }
    is CanProvisionResult.CannotBeProvisioned.ApiError,
    is CanProvisionResult.CannotBeProvisioned.Error,
    is CanProvisionResult.CannotBeProvisioned.UnknownFailure -> { /* show error */ }
}

val provisionResult = cardProvisioning.provision(
    cardDisplayName = "Adyen Business Card",
    cardAddress = CardAddress(),
    opcProvider = { paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput ->
        // Backend call 2: POST networkTokenActivationData with sdkOutput -> card data
        sdkBackend.requestOpaquePaymentCardData(paymentInstrumentId, sdkOutput).sdkInput
    },
)

docs.title: After — Card Provisioning Sessions
docs.text:
@file:OptIn(AdyenExperimentalApi::class)

import com.adyen.issuing.mobile.provisioning.client.annotation.AdyenExperimentalApi

val createResult = ProvisioningSession.create(
    context = applicationContext,
    configuration = ProvisioningSessionConfiguration(
        appCertificate = appCertificate, // DER-encoded bytes of the .cer from Adyen
        paymentInstrumentIds = setOf(paymentInstrumentId),
        // The SDK environment must match the token endpoint the backend calls:
        // Live pairs with https://authe-live.adyen.com, Test with https://test.adyen.com.
        environment = SessionEnvironment.Live   // default
    ),
    activityProvider = { hostingActivity },
    tokenProvider = { paymentInstrumentIds ->
        // Single backend call: the endpoint requests a token from Adyen's session API
        SessionToken(sessionsBackend.fetchToken(paymentInstrumentIds))
    },
)
val session = (createResult as ProvisioningSessionCreateResult.Success).session

when (session.provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId)) {
    ProvisioningState.CanProvision -> { /* show Add to Wallet */ }
    ProvisioningState.Provisioned -> { /* already in wallet — hide button */ }
    // ... see Result-type changes below for the CannotProvision variants to handle
    is ProvisioningState.CannotProvision -> { /* show reason */ }
}

val provisionResult = session.provisionCard(
    paymentInstrumentId = paymentInstrumentId,
    cardDisplayName = "Adyen Business Card",
    cardAddress = CardAddress(),
)

The CardAddress import does not change — it is defined in the offline provisioning SDK's client.data package and re-used unchanged by the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK.

docs.title: Result-type changes
docs.text:
The Session-based result types intentionally expose a different, more focused failure surface than the offline provisioning SDK because operational concerns the offline provisioning SDK delegates to your backend (token retrieval, session establishment, activation-data handling, tamper detection) become observable inside the SDK once it manages the session.

ProvisioningSessionCreateResult — replaces CardProvisioningCreateResult:

Card Provisioning (Offline) Card Provisioning Sessions Success(cardProvisioning) Success(session) Failed.GooglePayNotSupported No counterpart at creation — wallet support now surfaces as ProvisioningState.CannotProvision.WalletNotSupported or ProvisionResult.Failure.TapAndPayNotAvailable Failed.InvalidSdkInput No counterpart — there is no opaque sdkInput payload anymore (none) Failure.ApplicationCertificateError — the appCertificate bytes could not be parsed as X.509 (none) Failure.Error(message: String?) — any other creation failure with optional reason

ProvisioningState — replaces CanProvisionResult for the eligibility check:

Card Provisioning (Offline) Card Provisioning Sessions CanBeProvisioned CanProvision CannotBeProvisioned.AlreadyExistsInWallet Provisioned — a positive state rather than a failure: there is nothing left to do for this card CannotBeProvisioned.ApiError(statusCode) CannotProvision.ProvisioningFailed(message) CannotBeProvisioned.Error(throwable) CannotProvision.ProvisioningFailed(message) CannotBeProvisioned.UnknownFailure CannotProvision.ProvisioningFailed(message) (new) CannotProvision.CouldNotEstablishSession(message, traceId?) (new) CannotProvision.SessionTokenRetrievalFailed(message) (new) CannotProvision.ActivationDataUnavailable(message, traceId?) (new) CannotProvision.HttpError — sealed: Authentication(traceId, message?) for 401/403, Validation(traceId, message?) for 422, Server for 500 and other unexpected codes (new) CannotProvision.WalletNotSupported (new) CannotProvision.PaymentInstrumentNotAllowed (new) CannotProvision.TamperError(tamperCode)

Sessions ProvisionResult.Failure — supersedes the SDK's failure set:

Variant Notes PaymentInstrumentNotAllowed The id is not in the session's set AlreadyProvisioned Card is already in the wallet ProvisioningCancelled User cancelled Google's provisioning flow ProvisioningAlreadyInProgress Another provisioning or wallet-creation operation is running in the application process, possibly for a different card; wait for it to finish TapAndPayNotAvailable The app cannot call the Tap and Pay API CouldNotEstablishSession(message, traceId?) The secure session with the Adyen backend could not be established SessionTokenRetrievalFailed(message) The SessionTokenProvider threw an exception or returned an unusable token ActivationDataUnavailable(message, traceId?) Activation data could not be retrieved or processed HttpError — sealed: Authentication(traceId, message?) for 401/403, Validation(traceId, message?) for 422, Server for 500 and other unexpected codes An HTTP error occurred while communicating with the Adyen backend ProvisioningFailed(message) Unexpected SDK or wallet failure — the catch-all for the offline provisioning SDK's many Google Play service and tokenization failure variants TamperError(tamperCode) A RASP violation was detected and the request was blocked

docs.title: Trace IDs and HTTP errors
docs.text:
CouldNotEstablishSession, ActivationDataUnavailable, and HttpError include an optional traceId. Share it with Adyen support to help locate the failed backend request. It comes from the response's traceparent header and is null if that header is missing or invalid.

HttpError has three variants:

  • Authentication — HTTP 401 or 403.
  • Validation — HTTP 422.
  • Server — HTTP 500 or any other unexpected non-2xx status.

Authentication and Validation include decrypted backend error text in message when available; otherwise it is null. Server.message contains fixed support guidance rather than backend error text. See handling the final state for details.

Most of these variants map to a small set of UI states for typical applications (retryable transport error, non-retryable validation error, terminal "card is already in wallet"), but the Kotlin compiler will require each branch to be addressed explicitly when a when expression is exhaustive.

docs.title: What remains unchanged
docs.text:
• Google Push Provisioning API allowlisting. Both SDKs rely on Google's Push Provisioning API and the same allowlisting steps apply. See Google Push Provisioning API Access. Existing allowlisting for Google's legacy Tap and Pay push-provisioning API does not carry over to Unified Push Provisioning (UPP). If your app was previously approved for the legacy API, request allowlisting again for UPP before using SDK version 0.6.0 or later. From release 0.6.0, play-services-tapandpay is bundled inside the published provisioning-sdk artifact, so neither SDK requires you to host the library yourself.
  • CardAddress. Same fields, same package, no migration required.
  • activityProvider: () -> Activity. The lambda is invoked in the same way; pass the host Activity as before. It is called on demand (not at factory time), so it must always resolve to the currently-resumed Activity. Do not rely on a failure result to detect a destroyed Activity; keep the provider lifecycle-aware. See Lifecycle guidance for recommended patterns.
  • @AdyenExperimentalApi. Both SDKs require the same opt-in annotation at call sites.
  • Minimum Android API and compileSdk requirements. Unchanged at API 26 / compileSdk 36.

docs.title: Step-by-step migration
docs.text:
1. Add the new dependency:

    dependencies {
    implementation("com.adyen.issuing.provisioning:provisioning-sessions:0.6.0")
}

  2. Embed the application certificate. Place the certificate provided by Adyen in res/raw/ (or another readable location) and load its DER-encoded bytes so they can be passed to ProvisioningSession.create(...) inside a ProvisioningSessionConfiguration.

  3. Implement the session-token backend endpoint that proxies to Adyen's session API and returns the issued token. Integrate it into the client behind a SessionTokenProvider that wraps the token in a SessionToken. See Fetch a Session Token for the request format.

  4. Update the repository or use-case to use the Session-based flow, replacing the existing call sites using the API mapping. The example app's ProvisioningSessionsRepository is a reference for the new flow.

  5. Update the error mapping to cover the ProvisioningState and ProvisionResult branches. Treat the backend-related variants conservatively — retry where transport-related; otherwise surface the failure and abort. Always handle TamperError explicitly by invalidating the session on your backend.

  6. Decommission the old API surface after migrating to the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK: remove the direct dependency on the offline provisioning SDK, delete the OpcProvider integration code, and retire the two networkTokenActivationData backend endpoints if no other consumers remain.

docs.title: 1. Require User Authentication
docs.text:
Ask the user to confirm their identity before sensitive operations such as adding a card to Google Wallet. For device biometrics or PIN, pattern, or password authentication, you can use BiometricPrompt from AndroidX Biometric, as shown below, or an equivalent flow provided by another authentication library.

The example below creates the prompt when authentication starts, which keeps it short. A prompt delivers its result to the Activity that created it. If the Activity can be recreated while the prompt is showing, for example after rotation, create the BiometricPrompt in onCreate() and call only authenticate() from your action. Otherwise, the replacement Activity does not receive the result.

fun requireAuthentication(activity: FragmentActivity, onAuthenticated: () -> Unit) {
    // Strong biometrics combined with the device credential is supported from Android 11 (API 30).
    val authenticators = if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.R) {
        BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG or BiometricManager.Authenticators.DEVICE_CREDENTIAL
    } else {
        BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_WEAK or BiometricManager.Authenticators.DEVICE_CREDENTIAL
    }
    if (BiometricManager.from(activity).canAuthenticate(authenticators) != BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_SUCCESS) {
        // No screen lock or enrolled biometric: decide whether to block the operation.
        return
    }
    val prompt = BiometricPrompt(
        activity,
        ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(activity),
        object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() {
            override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(result: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) {
                onAuthenticated()
            }
        }
    )
    prompt.authenticate(
        BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder()
            .setTitle("Confirm it's you")
            .setAllowedAuthenticators(authenticators)
            .build()
    )
}

docs.title: 2. Prevent Screenshots and Screen Recording
docs.text:
Apply FLAG_SECURE to any Activity that displays sensitive SDK screens. This also prevents the screen appearing in the recent apps thumbnail.

override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    window.setFlags(
        WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE,
        WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE
    )
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_sensitive)
}

If you are using Jetpack Compose and every screen in the Activity is sensitive, set the flag in onCreate as shown above and do not clear it. If only some Compose screens are sensitive, count the screens that need the flag, so one screen leaving cannot clear it while another is still visible:

// Screens that currently need FLAG_SECURE, per window. Compose effects run on the main thread.
private val secureScreenCounts = WeakHashMap<Window, Int>()

@Composable
fun SensitiveScreen() {
    val window = LocalContext.current.findActivity().window
    DisposableEffect(window) {
        // If the Activity set the flag itself, never clear it from here.
        val managed = secureScreenCounts.containsKey(window) ||
            (window.attributes.flags and WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE) == 0
        if (managed) {
            secureScreenCounts[window] = (secureScreenCounts[window] ?: 0) + 1
            window.addFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE)
        }
        onDispose {
            if (managed) {
                val remaining = secureScreenCounts.getValue(window) - 1
                if (remaining == 0) {
                    secureScreenCounts.remove(window)
                    window.clearFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE)
                } else {
                    secureScreenCounts[window] = remaining
                }
            }
        }
    }
    // your content
}

// LocalContext can be a ContextWrapper (for example, a themed context), so unwrap it.
private tailrec fun Context.findActivity(): Activity = when (this) {
    is Activity -> this
    is ContextWrapper -> baseContext.findActivity()
    else -> error("SensitiveScreen must be hosted in an Activity")
}

Note: FLAG_SECURE does not prevent all forms of screen capture on rooted devices. For more information, see the Android documentation on window flags.

docs.title: 3. Store Credentials Securely
docs.text:
Do not store session tokens, API keys, or other credentials in plain SharedPreferences, files, or databases.

  • Keep Adyen API keys on your backend. Never ship an Adyen API key in your app.
  • Do not cache session tokens. The Sessions SDKs ask your SessionTokenProvider for a fresh token whenever they need one.
  • Encrypt anything sensitive you must store. Use a key held in the Android Keystore, and exclude the file from backup as described in Restrict Backup of Sensitive Data.

docs.title: 4. Restrict Backup of Sensitive Data
docs.text:
Android's auto-backup can inadvertently include sensitive SDK data. Disable backup entirely or use backup rules to exclude sensitive files. See the Android documentation on Backing up app data for details.

In your AndroidManifest.xml:

<application
    android:allowBackup="false"
    ... >

If you allow backup for other app data, exclude the Sessions SDKs' encrypted DataStore files: device_id_store, os_version_store, and signature_store, all directly under filesDir (backup domain file). These contain device-bound state and must not be restored onto another device. Add separate exclusions for any sensitive files your application creates; the rules below cover only SDK-managed files.

For Android 11 and lower, use res/xml/backup_rules.xml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<full-backup-content>
    <exclude domain="file" path="device_id_store" />
    <exclude domain="file" path="os_version_store" />
    <exclude domain="file" path="signature_store" />
</full-backup-content>

For Android 12 and higher, exclude the same files from both cloud backup and device transfer in res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml. Some manufacturers allow device transfer even with allowBackup="false", so configure these rules explicitly.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<data-extraction-rules>
    <cloud-backup>
        <exclude domain="file" path="device_id_store" />
        <exclude domain="file" path="os_version_store" />
        <exclude domain="file" path="signature_store" />
    </cloud-backup>
    <device-transfer>
        <exclude domain="file" path="device_id_store" />
        <exclude domain="file" path="os_version_store" />
        <exclude domain="file" path="signature_store" />
    </device-transfer>
</data-extraction-rules>

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<application
    android:fullBackupContent="@xml/backup_rules"
    android:dataExtractionRules="@xml/data_extraction_rules"
    ... >

docs.title: 5. Handle Sensitive Data in Memory Carefully
docs.text:
Avoid passing sensitive values (tokens and keys) as String objects where possible, as strings are immutable and cannot be zeroed out after use. Prefer CharArray or ByteArray so you can explicitly clear them when done.

Never log sensitive values, even in debug builds:

// ❌ Never do this
Log.d("SDK", "User token: $token")

// Log an event without token content or token-derived metadata.
Log.d("SDK", "Session token received")

docs.title: 6. Use Secure Networking
docs.text:
Use HTTPS for every call between your app and your backend, including the session token and activation data requests. From Android 9 (API 28), apps block cleartext HTTP by default. Do not re-enable it with android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" or a permissive network security configuration:

<!-- res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" />
</network-security-config>

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<application
    android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config"
    ... >

For extra protection against man-in-the-middle attacks on your own backend, consider certificate pinning with a <pin-set> in the same configuration. Include a backup pin and set an expiration, so a certificate rotation cannot lock users out of your app.

docs.title: 7. Respond to Tamper Signals
docs.text:
The Adyen Issuing SDKs perform Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) checks at sensitive call sites (see the Environment Constraints section of the main README). In the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK, when a threat is detected (root, hooking, memory scanning, emulator, virtual environment, compromised hardware, or a debugger attached to a release build), the SDK stops performing sensitive work and returns a TamperError result to your code.

The client-side SDK intentionally does not wipe keys or cached state on tamper detection:

  • Session private keys are generated in hardware-backed Android Keystore (StrongBox / TEE), which is designed to prevent key export. This does not guarantee that a compromised process cannot invoke a key or observe plaintext around its use.
  • Persisted state is encrypted with device-bound Keystore keys and is not portable to another device.
  • An attacker capable of bypassing RASP could equally hook out any client-side wipe logic, so "refuse to operate" is a stronger invariant than "try to delete".

Because of this, server-side session invalidation is your responsibility. When an SDK call returns a TamperError variant, treat it as a cue to terminate the user's session on your backend (logout, session revoke, risk flag) so the session token is refused regardless of what the compromised client does next. Combine this with short-lived session tokens and server-side rate-limiting for defence-in-depth.

Example for the Card Provisioning Sessions SDK:

when (val result = provisioningSession.provisioningState(paymentInstrumentId)) {
    is ProvisioningState.CannotProvision.TamperError -> {
        // Invalidate the user's session on your backend, then surface a
        // neutral "unable to continue" UI. Do not hint at the reason.
        backend.invalidateSession()
        showGenericErrorAndLogOut()
    }
    // … handle other result variants
    else -> { /* … */ }
}

The same pattern applies to ProvisionResult.Failure.TamperError returned from provisionCard.

Do not surface the specific tamper reason to the user — a neutral error message avoids giving attackers feedback on which check triggered.

docs.title: 8. Prevent Tapjacking and Overlay Attacks
docs.text:
Tapjacking tricks users into tapping UI elements hidden beneath a malicious overlay. Filter out touch events that have been obscured by another window. For more information see the Android documentation on Tapjacking.

Apply this to any View handling sensitive interactions, such as confirmation buttons:

sensitiveButton.setOnTouchListener { view, event ->
    val obscured = MotionEvent.FLAG_WINDOW_IS_OBSCURED or
        MotionEvent.FLAG_WINDOW_IS_PARTIALLY_OBSCURED // API 29+; safe no-op on earlier devices
    if (event.flags and obscured != 0) {
        // Touch event obscured by an overlay — reject it
        return@setOnTouchListener true
    }
    view.onTouchEvent(event)
}

Or apply it globally across your Activity by overriding dispatchTouchEvent:

override fun dispatchTouchEvent(event: MotionEvent): Boolean {
    val obscured = MotionEvent.FLAG_WINDOW_IS_OBSCURED or
        MotionEvent.FLAG_WINDOW_IS_PARTIALLY_OBSCURED
    if (event.flags and obscured != 0) {
        return false
    }
    return super.dispatchTouchEvent(event)
}

You can also declare this in XML on individual Views:

<Button
    android:filterTouchesWhenObscured="true"
    ... />

docs.title: 9. Verify Release Builds Are Not Debuggable
docs.text: Ensure your release build is not debuggable. A debuggable app allows attackers to attach a debugger, inspect memory, and bypass security checks. The Android Gradle Plugin sets isDebuggable = false by default for the release build type, but you should verify it is not accidentally overridden or inherited in custom build types.

docs.title: 10. Protect Exported Components
docs.text:
Ensure Activities, Services, and Receivers that are not intended for external use are not exported. Any exported component is a potential entry point for attack.

<!-- Unexported — internal use only -->
<activity
    android:name=".SensitiveActivity"
    android:exported="false" />

<!-- If a component must be exported, restrict with a signature-level permission -->
<activity
    android:name=".DeeplinkActivity"
    android:exported="true"
    android:permission="com.yourapp.permission.DEEPLINK" />

<permission
    android:name="com.yourapp.permission.DEEPLINK"
    android:protectionLevel="signature" />

docs.title: 11. Secure WebViews
docs.text:
If your integration uses WebViews, apply the following hardening. See the Android Web App Security documentation for a complete overview.

webView.settings.apply {
    javaScriptEnabled = true // only if strictly required
    allowFileAccess = false
    allowContentAccess = false
    allowFileAccessFromFileURLs = false
    allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs = false
    setSupportMultipleWindows(false)
    javaScriptCanOpenWindowsAutomatically = false
}

// Remove interfaces not in use
webView.removeJavascriptInterface("searchBoxJavaBridge_")
webView.removeJavascriptInterface("accessibility")
webView.removeJavascriptInterface("accessibilityTraversal")

// Restrict navigation to known hosts
webView.webViewClient = object : WebViewClient() {
    override fun shouldOverrideUrlLoading(view: WebView, request: WebResourceRequest): Boolean {
        val host = request.url.host ?: return true
        return if (host.equals("your-trusted-domain.com", ignoreCase = true) || host.endsWith(".your-trusted-domain.com", ignoreCase = true)) {
            false // allow
        } else {
            true // block
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 12. ProGuard and R8 Configuration
docs.text:
Ensure minification is enabled in your release builds. The SDK ships with its own consumer ProGuard rules, but verify your setup keeps R8 active:

buildTypes {
    release {
        isMinifyEnabled = true
        isShrinkResources = true
    }
}

If you are using any SDK models in your own ProGuard rules, only keep rules that are strictly necessary. Overly broad -keep rules will undo obfuscation and make reverse engineering easier. For detailed documentation on setting up code shrinking and obfuscation, see the Android Shrink, obfuscate, and optimize your app documentation.

# ❌ Too broad — avoid
-keep class com.example.** { *; }

# ✅ Keep only what your code references directly
-keep class com.example.sdk.MySdk { public *; }

For advanced security and obfuscation beyond what R8 provides, you may want to consider using a commercial application protection product such as DexGuard, Appdome, or Promon. These tools offer features like string encryption, class encryption, and runtime application self-protection (RASP).
